subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FOURTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE

speechtext: The house resumed, from Thursday, December 12, consideration of the motion of Mr. Blair that the fourth report of the special committee on procedure of the house, presented to the house on Friday, December 6, 1968, be concurred in, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Stanfield (p. 3762).

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FOURTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the debate was adjourned last night I had made reference to the remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on Tuesday evening, as reported at page 3787 of Hansard, in describing the business transacted so far in the current session. The Prime Minister said:
In this session we have already allowed three months to go by and only passed nine measures.
Then I went on to described some of the events in the house over the past three months. I noted that in fact some 35 or more days had been absorbed by house business involving important items such as the throne speech debate, the budget debate, all the items of supply and the establishment of the

two procedure committees. I went on to outline the very valid use of time in considering the legislation that has been presented by the government to date.
In my view it would be regrettable if the Prime Minister, his cabinet ministers or other members were to leave the faulty impression that parliament has been dragging its feet. It should be noted that parliament has disposed of the following items of business, regardless of whether members agreed or disagreed in part or in whole with any or all of the particular measures that have been disposed of.
First of all, the throne speech was completed in less than the allotted time. It is important that this debate be maintained because it affords members on both sides of the house the opportunity to debate the state of the nation. I disagree with those who suggest that this debate is of little value. It affords all members the opportunity to take an over-all view of Canada's affairs and also to present specific problems of importance to their own constituencies. If for any reason the debate on the speech from the throne dragged this year, then with all respect I would suggest that this was due, first of all, to the warmed-over soup that was dished up in the speech from the throne and, second, to the dishwater type of presentation made by cabinet ministers in dealing with the issues facing the country. Only the Prime Minister and three cabinet ministers chose to take part in the debate and to present any ideas about the new society of which we have heard so much.
The second item of business disposed of was the presentation of the budget and the budget debate. This is one item that was delayed as a result of the Prime Minister's decision to call an election. The budget can be regarded as the single most important item of business to be dealt with during a session. Considering the impact of the budget on the economy, debate is critical. In fact, a good case can be made for saying that the time allotted to the debate this year was inadequate, that further time was required.
The third item was the passage of interim supply. Again this was necessary because of the dissolution of parliament earlier this year. Matters that were debated at that time did require further debate.
The fourth item dealt with was passage of supply for 1968-69. I am sure members will agree that the voting of some $10 billion worth of expenditures is a major and most important item of business. The present procedures provide for a specified period of
December 13, 19S8

time for the consideration of supply. I am sure most hon. members agree that the discussion carried on during this period is useful and needed. New procedures for handling supply are now being proposed and I share the doubts of many members in regard to them. Nevertheless, I am prepared to try these new procedures, subject to adequate consideration of them now and a further review in the future.
The fifth item disposed of was the establishment of the procedure committee and the committee on statutory instruments. Debate was essential because of the importance of the operations of parliament, which is a critical factor in the functioning of democracy as has been demonstrated by the debate that is now under way.
The sixth item was passage of one private bill and limited consideration of other private bills and resolutions. I recognize that consideration of these measures comes under the heading of private members' business. However, we must not lose sight of the fact that these measures are an important part of the business of parliament.
The seventh area dealt with was passage of the Farm Credit Act amendments. This was a controversial piece of legislation and considerable debate on it took place. Indeed, there will continue to be debate on the real value of the measure which was passed. Nevertheless, it was passed and I am sure government members are now trying to take some credit for it wherever that is possible. If extensive time was used for that debate I suggest it was not only due to the controversial nature of the subject matter but also to the unwillingness of the government to provide information on the matters under discussion until it was pried out of them in lengthy debate.
The eighth item was passage of the Farm Improvement Loans Act amendments. Again this legislation was controversial and will continue to be a source of controversy. Regardless of the views that we hold about it it must be regarded as an item of business that has now been disposed of by this house.
We also dealt with the Post Office Act amendments, the Publication of Statutes Act, which was certainly regarded as an important measure, a Canadian National Railways branch line construction bill which was given priority by the government, as was the Judges Act, the Canadian National Railways financing bill, which was important, and lastly the Customs Tariff Act. When that act was introduced in the house by the parliamentary

Motion for Concurrence in Report secretary to the Minister of Finance he described it as being of historic significance to Canada.
Finally, we completed the resolution stage of the official languages bill, the amendments to the Bretton Woods Agreements Act and to the Farm Machinery Syndicates Credit Act. We have also had part or all of the minister's speech on second reading of the bill to amend the Patent Act, the Trade Marks Act and the Food and Drugs Act, as well as the minister's speech on the resolution to establish the freshwater fish marketing board.
Whether I happen to agree with all or part of the measures that have been passed is immaterial to the point now under consideration. The point is that these are major items of business that have been disposed of by the house. In fact, I could spin out the list even further because other items might also be included. Not without note is the work of some of the committees and the prior steps that are required to be taken by parliament to put the committees to work. Any suggestions by the Prime Minister or other hon. members which would deliberately downgrade the work of this parliament would be a disservice to this house and constitute a misrepresentation to the country.

During this debate the operation of our parliament has been compared with the operation of the parliament at Westminster. In any such discussion we must keep in mind that the two parliaments are of different size; here we have 264 members and at Westminster they have 625 members. Also, England for the most part may be termed a homogeneous country in which geographic factors play a limited part. The English government is a unitary government. On the other hand, Canada is much larger and is split up into basic physical and economic regions. We have a federal government. There are differences in the operations of unitary and federal governments. Certainly our federal type of government means that government work may become more complex, and that will be reflected in parliamentary work at all stages. Because of the complexity of the considerations any parliament in Canada must deal with and because of the many viewpoints which must be heard in debate in this country it is necessary to remember that there is a significant difference in the make-up of the Canadian and British parliaments.

For instance, the people of Britain at the present time have decided that they want to be represented in their parliament by two parties, the third party being very small in terms of the number of members in that parliament. On the other hand, the people of Canada have decided that they want four parties basically to represent them at present in parliament. Regardless of the views of hon. members on the subject or whether they want this situation or not, this is what the people of Canada have decided. Parliament must therefore recognize the existence of several bodies of thought in this nation with differing political viewpoints.
A good deal has been said about the organization of house business. The hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Deachman) in particular referred to the lack of organization of the business of the house. Some hon. members have implied that the opposition is opposed to planning the business of the house. I think we all recognize that there is a need to plan the operations of the house and if one looks at the wording of the amendment that is before us one will see that the principle of the need to plan the business of the house is accepted.
May I direct the attention of hon. members to part of the wording of the amendment before us. It recommends:
-that proposed standing order 16-A be amended to provide that a motion to accept the decision of the proceedings committee shall only be made following the unanimous decision of the proceedings committee arrived at during a meeting properly convened upon adequate written notice.
The wording of the amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition shows that we accept the principle that we must organize and plan the business of the house. What is proposed here is a change in the method or the mechanics of the operation which is essential to the fulfilment of that proposition. To judge from the remarks of some hon. members it appears they have not read the amendment or have not given it adequate consideration.
Reference has been made to the necessity of allowing more time in the house for the transaction of government business. I confess some sympathy with this point of view. I note that some hon. members have said that on some days after the house completed its routine business there was not much time left for the consideration of government business. It must be recognized that provision has been made to extend the opportunities under

which the government may present its proposals to the house.
Some hon. members have spoken of the preliminary business of the house and orders of the day in a way which suggests they want these parts of the procedures of the house discontinued or diminished. The committee concluded, it seems to me, that the time taken on orders of the day is a valid use of the time of the house, and that questions on urgent matters ought to be presented. I trust that thon. members on the government side do not question the right of hon. members to ask the government questions on urgent matters.
A number of hon. members also spoke of private members' business and I agree with some suggestions put forward. We ought to consider changes which will make private members' discussions more meaningful. That part of the business of the house is important and we should not sacrifice it for the sake of allowing more time to be devoted to government business.
The proposed rule changes provide for added hours of sitting. They provide for the transfer of some items now before the house to committees and they also provide for the elimination of the resolution stage. On many of these matters most hon. members are in agreement. All the same, I do not think we ought to provide more time for government business at the expense of the rights of private members. We must consider the rights of private members, the backbenchers on both sides of the house. That those rights exist has been recognized by eminent authorities. I will not take time to quote from the well known work of MacGregor Dawson entitled "The Government of Canada" on the rights of private members of the house, but he says that those rights must be carefully considered and balanced against the needs of the government.
The principle contained in proposed standing order 16-A recognizes the need for the planning of the business of the house. Hon. members opposite do not seem to have supported the principle of planning in the past; yet now we find them in favour of it. Of course, if planning is carried out in a heavyhanded, authoritarian way it can be undemocratic. If proposed standing order 16-A as now worded is implemented, certainly that is the direction in which we shall be headed. The government seems to have mastered the technique of handling planning procedures and has gone ahead in a heavyhanded way to bring in the proposal now before us. This is not right. Of course planning can be carried out democratically if there is a process of

consultation-free collective bargaining, in effect-and finally agreement. When there is no agreement the differences in our various political philosophies come into play, of course, and then those differences must be debated. Controversial issues must be debated. Yet the question still remains, who is to say when we have had enough debate? Certainly the decision of that question should not be left to one side of the house or the other.
Much of what I have said has been said from the viewpoint of one newly elected to this house. I did not secure election to the House of Commons to participate in the strangling of this institution. I came here to participate in debate on the issues facing this nation and, after adequate discussion, to participate in decisions on proposals before this house. Standing order 16-A as presented does not meet this standard. For that reason I urge hon. members to vote in favour of the amendment now before us in order to ensure that a job partly done is well done.

In 1963 the estimates of several departments went through without hardly a word being said despite the fact that a number of hon. members had questions to ask about them. The right hon. gentleman was prime minister in early 1963, and in January and February of that year he ran into a problem because far too much time was being taken on the estimates. The house was still voting interim supply although ten-twelfths or eleven-twelfths of the money had been spent. With this in mind, I am sure the right hon. gentleman will support my contention that this is not a good situation.
There are many advantages attached to referring estimates to standing committees. We know that when the estimates of the Department of Agriculture, the Department of External Affairs or any other department are before a committee of this house there is a fairly low attendance. But the members who are present are members who have specialized in the work of the department and who therefore take a keen interest in the debate which is taking place. However, if it is necessary to put all the estimates through the committee of supply and if members are obliged to stand in line waiting to speak, there is bound to be a great waste of time. It is now being proven that four or five standing committees can function concurrently reasonably well. This provides an opportunity for backbenchers and, indeed, for ministers, to attend the committees in which they are particularly interested and to question the senior officials of the department concerned as well as other witnesses, a most useful exercise in relation to what happens here on the floor of the house.
The 15th report of the special committee on procedure was introduced into this house on December 14, 1964. There are several members in the opposition who were on that committee. Moreover, no majority reports were

filed; these were unanimous reports and it is therefore not possible for any hon. member who was on the committee to say he disagreed with the recommendations the particular report to which I have referred will be found in Votes and Proceedings for December 14, 1964. I quote:
Your committee is of the opinion that the potential value of the committe system of the House of Commons is not being exploited to the full, particularly in relation to standing committees. The structure of the standing committees tends to be cumbersome and, in some respects, even archaic. Your committee is convinced that a fundamental reorganization of standing committees is necessary if they are to be revitalized and their effectiveness and prestige enhanced.

Your committee recommends that not more than 20 days be set aside for debating the main estimates in committee of supply. On such days it should be the right of the opposition to select the departments for discussion.

I know there were some additional days for supply motions and that sort of thing, but what is being suggested here in the present report from the committee is 25 days. Secondly, I believe some of these specific proposals are dangerous. I think some are ineffective in their present form; others are foreign to our particular system of parliamentary democracy.
During my years in parliament I have never become, as have some of my colleagues, an expert on the rules and procedures of the house. I cannot even claim to have taken any particular interest in this subject in the past. But recent events and the circumstances of the present have forced me to make myself, if not an expert, then keenly aware of the vital importance of this question.
The reasons for this is simple. Like the people who elected me to represent them here, I hold a strong attachment to the system of government that we know as British parliamentary democracy. This system may have defects, it may falter and creak on occasion. But what free system of government operated by ordinary men and women does not have weaknesses? Surely the important question is to decide which system has the fewest weaknesses; and I believe the answer is "our system".
A leading authority on government, a man who was never, in my opinion, under any circumstances described as a Conservative, was Harold J. Laski. He opened his great work "Parliamentary Government in England" with these words:
No system of representative government has a history so continuous or so successful as that of Great Britain.
I believe this is true. I believe in the effectiveness of our system. Like the majority of my fellow Canadians I believe in its effectiveness to provide good, stable, democratic government. I further believe in its ability to protect the rights of the individual and of minorities from abuse by an autocratic executive. I believe in parliament's historic role of servant, not master, of the citizen. It is because I suspect that there are those among us who would use the device of procedural reform as a cover for their real purpose that I am so concerned. It is because I suspect that these proposed reforms are a first step toward a fundamental change in the system of government in this country that I have been forced to take a close and keen interest in this question.
December 13, 1968	COMMONS
Those who propose these changes now before us claim they do so only to make parliament more modern, more efficient, more able to cope with the demands of today's world. This is a reasonable claim. Though it is reasonable, it is not necessarily sound; and it is only reasonable if it is made in good faith. But so many things have been happening in recent months, there have been so many warning signs, that I believe it would be wise for all of us here to look beyond the mere mechanics of procedural change.
I think of the "ministerial Mafia" that was uncovered in the gallery yesterday. Surely, Mr. Speaker, it is better to indulge suspicions that later on may turn out to be groundless than to rush to adopt changes that we may find have emasculated parliament and opened the door to an alien, perhaps even sinister, system of government.
It could happen-I do not say it must-that there are those in this country who seek to do by stealth and deception what they know they could not achieve by an open and democratic expression of public opinion. Anyone dedicated to changing our form of government might well feel the fastest and easiest way to do so would be to weaken, distort and discredit our present institution.
I am appalled by the philosophy, so often and so brashly exemplified by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald), that belittles the role of this house as a forum of free discussion and reduces it to a mere appendage of a sealed legislative machine. Today's political technocrats regard the House of Commons as an industrial machine to be urged to higher and ever higher production levels until it spews forth an endless flow of new laws. This view makes completely meaningless our democratic electoral system. Some hon. members may remember the great satire on mass production, the movie "Modern Times." This measure makes of members of parliament so many Charlie Chaplins humbly serving the machine.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
What makes the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald) so sure that they have all the moral values, all the wisdom and all honour that exists in this house? A British writer writing in the Spectator in the 1930's, when dictatorship was in fashion, was discussing the popular claim that dictators and dictatorships were more efficient, more effective and speedier than free parliaments and constitutional executives. Dr. G. P. Gooch said it was
DEBATES	3937
Motion for Concurrence in Report claimed that dictatorships could deliver the goods; but he asked, what sort of goods, and at what sort of price? This might be a good question to ask ourselves today when we are being urged to become more swift and efficient at the cost of open debate and free discussion. I do not believe that any such sudden and drastic change in our rules and procedures can be warranted on the grounds only of speed and efficiency.
I do not wish to burden you or the record, Mr. Speaker, with too many quotations but I feel that in this debate one ought to put on record as many opinions as possible, particularly when those opinions carry the weight of study and experience which have been denied to the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Macdonald).
Professor Reginald G. Bassett, the professor of political science at the London School of Economics until his death in 1962, is considered by many to be an outstanding modern authority on the system we know as parliamentary democracy. His book The Essentials of Parliamentary Democracy is a standard reference work. Among other things he wrote:
There are some democrats who claim that parliamentary democracy can be speeded up to such an extent that decisions can be taken as quickly as under dictatorships. That, in our view, is a delusion. Democratic government must be comparatively slow in the taking of decisions: that is the price which has to be paid for political freedom.
He also noted:
Taking of decisions is one thing, and lasting achievement quite another.
He was concerned with the danger to the system of shallow proposals for change and hasty decisions difficult to reverse, once made. This is what he wrote:
More dangerous, perhaps, in present circumstances, than either the impatience of the extreme left or the obstinacy of the extreme right, is the demand for action as such.
He saw little virtue in change for the sake of change and action for the sake of action, and added:
To desire speed for its own sake is irrational, and, in politics, as in other spheres of human activity, the indulgence of such a desire may have regrettable consequences.
Before I leave this particular aspect of the debate, Mr. Speaker, I will cite just one more authority. Right Hon. Michael Stewart in his book The British Approach to Politics, wrote:
-it would be unwise to pursue efficiency at the expense of individuality. Parliament is more than
December 13, 1968

Motion for Concurrence in Report a machine for making laws; it is a forum for discussion, for redress of grievances and exposure of abuses.
This, Mr. Speaker, exactly sets out one of the chief reasons why I deplore this government's obvious attempt to drive debate out of this chamber and into the back rooms.
In looking for the real purpose underlying these proposed changes we should look at the whole tenor of parliament, at the tone of parliament, as set by this new government. The tenor generally speaking-and I say this regretfully-has been one that demeans the House of Commons. We have only to consider the preposterous duty roster of ministers initiated by the Prime Minister. It is a clownish device at which one might laugh, if its implications were not so serious. I view it as a deliberate attempt to restrict the accountability of the executive to the people, to protect ministers arbitrarily from proper questioning and to humiliate and deliberately to degrade the House of Commons and render the role of elected representatives a farce.

speechtext: Shame.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FOURTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
It may be, of course, that the Prime Minister has banished his ministers to the cabinet harem because he is jealous of their ability, or fears their facility for putting their feet in their mouths. Whatever his reason for cloistering the cabinet, he has shown contempt of his colleagues and of parliament, and I think this attitude of contempt for parliament is reflected clearly in these proposed changes in our rules and procedures.
The Prime Minister's attitude in this house and in many of his public utterances indicates that he holds parliament in contempt as a mere talking shop. He likes to be portrayed as a political sophisticate. Professor Laski, who is an older and wiser hand at this business, once wrote:
It has become almost the proof of political sophistication to sneer at the House. The 'talking shop' leads many people to sigh, like Carlyle, for Colonel Pride and his little platoon. On all this there are many things to be said: not least of them that the alternative to the 'talking shop' is the concentration camp.
The other evening, on December 10, I believe, the Prime Minister gave an interview in which he said, among other things, that the opposition was holding up the business of the country by debating the rule changes. I ask, what business is being held up? What fundamental and earth-shaking steps to formulate the just society are being held up?

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FOURTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: What are they?

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FOURTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, what are they? Is one of the measures the measure to increase interest rates for fishermen's loans, perhaps? Or could it be a bill to amend the Historic Sites and Monuments Act, or a measure to arrest the spread of pests injurious to plants? If these are the vital and important measures that are being held up by this discussion of proposed changes in our rules and procedures, Mr. Speaker, I suggest they give a very clear understanding of the importance attached by the Prime Minister to these changes and to parliament. If the Prime Minister had signified his government's intention to bring forward measures dealing with the really crucial aspects of the nation's business, by placing appropriate measures on the order paper, he would have been more convincing. Where are the measures to deal with such urgent matters as unemployment, the steadily rising cost of living, the plight of eastern farmers, the grave crisis in western grain, and the desperate condition of the east coast fishing industry? No, these cannot be found among the priority matters on the government slate. Instead we have such pressing measures as an official languages bill, and changes in the rules of the house.
A giant step towards making parliament more effective could be taken by having this government give priority to the proper national questions. The Prime Minister has changed the face of this house by arbitrarily ordering his ministers to stay out of it. He has set up a system of regional desks within his own office to partition the national business regionally, and to further remove national business from his colleagues and the Commons.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
He has suggested that perhaps more frequent use of the name of the Governor General might be made in connection with legislation, rather than that of the Queen. The logical next step for him to take in this regard, one might fear, is to forget about the Governor General and use the name of a president yet to be named by him.
These are all straws in the wind, signs and portents that show the drift of national affairs under this regime. Now we have a suggestion to chase public business out of the open chamber and into the back rooms of parliament. We have a suggestion for the autocratic allotment of time for debate by a government
December 13, 1968

unimpeded by rules or an effective opposition. The whole trend is to get away from the public eye and into the citadel of absolute parliamentary power. I am afraid, Mr. Speaker, that the ultimate step could be a declaration of a form of government modelled on that of France, where parliament would be the powerless and subservient tool of a north American de Gaulle.
Would you believe "General" Trudeau? Before anyone laughs too loudly, let him remember that last February it was the present Prime Minister, then minister of justice, who said: "We are the masters." I do not know whether my suspicions are shared by all or any of my colleagues here, or by Canadians outside this house; but I feel they are valid until disproved, and I say that in the national interest it would be well if the Prime Minister were to make a clear and public undertaking that the intention of this government in advancing these changes had no connection with the intention eventually to change our parliamentary democracy into a republican form of government.
Before I finish my remarks I should like to take up one point of specific objection to these proposals. It has to do with the apparent failure of the government to make the necessary adjustments to our committee system to accommodate its proposed use of committees. In Britain, as I understand it, the practice is to refer bills to an appropriate committee after second reading, much as is suggested by the proposal now before us, in accordance with which proceedings at the committee stage, formerly handled in committee of the whole house, would be dealt with in the same way but within the smaller confines of a standing committee.
It is true this is done in the United Kingdom, but the committee there is in every way a miniature replica of a committee of the whole house. Then again, this system is only possible because the British committee is not an investigative, but a legislative committee. The purpose of the standing and special committees of this house, as now constituted, is set out in section 8 of the proposed amendment to standing order 65. It is to examine and inquire into matters referred to them, to send for persons, documents and records, etc. In other words, the procedure of our committee, sitting as a replacement for the committee of the whole house on a bill, would be to call witnesses, ask questions, consider testimony and arrive at a report.
This would be completely contrary to the traditional procedure in the house at this

Motion for Concurrence in Report stage of a bill, and I submit it would be completely ineffective. When a bill is considered at the committee stage in the special legislative-type committee established in Great Britain, the procedure is an exact duplicate of the procedure we have known in committee of the whole house on a bill; the minister explains the various clauses, assisted by his departmental experts; the members ask questions, make their views known in speeches, and move amendments.
The manner in which our committees now proceed-and apparently nothing has been done to change it under these new proposals-is entirely different. They operate as an investigative body, with witnesses called and sworn, documents produced and members reduced to making their contributions by way of questions.
In the British committee no experts are heard-they must make their contributions through information passed either to the minister or to members on the other side. There is ample time for individual members to speak and be heard. I think this question of committee procedure should be cleared up before the house is asked to adopt a motion calling for the blanket assignment of legislation to these committees for consideration at a vital stage.

As soon as I am through.
I have many other reservations as to the effectiveness of the new system proposed. However, I am sure that other members, more skilled than I in the intricacies of the rules, will deal with them before this debate comes to an end. It does appear improbable, though, that the speed and efficiency so glibly promised by the President of the Privy Council will be forthcoming. After all, the personnel serving on the committees will be the same as the personnel of the house. With many committees sitting simultaneously, as they must if the promised speed up is to come about, we shall see members flying from one to another without adequate time for preparation, and amidst more confusion than you could shake a stick at.
I fail to see what advantage this proposed new system might have over the use of the whole house as a committee. As I have already stated, I am no expert on the rules but I cannot see what advantage is to be expected at this juncture. Indeed, I am almost inclined to believe that this change is being
3940	COMMONS
Motion for Concurrence in Report advocated simply because it might appear to be new and radical. I am reminded, Mr. Speaker, that Mussolini was defended on the ground that he produced greater efficiency. At least he made the trains run on time, it was said. Hitler was lauded for his efficiency in constructing superhighways. In neither case did the defenders of those dictators bother to mention for what purpose the railways and the roads were to be used.
From his many, one might even say endless, public statements about the need to turn parliament into a legislative mill, the President of the Privy Council would seem to be seeking immortality as the man who made parliament run. But in this case I think we would be very wise to ask also, to what end and for what purpose? I believe, Mr. Speaker, members of this house must ask themselves a question and assure themselves upon one main point before they saddle themselves with these proposed changes. We must assure ourselves that we are really trying to improve our system of government, not change our system of government. It is distinctly possible that by adopting these sweeping changes we will merely be accessories in preparing the ground for a fundamental change in the system.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
Sure, I may be charged with being an alarmist. I may be accused of bias and of many other things. But, Mr. Speaker, I smell republicanism in the air. I see some of its advocates in high places, and I hear its echoes in the statements of prominent members of the governing political party. Unless someone of the stature of the Prime Minister can effectively deodorize the atmosphere, the aroma is going to persist, and while it persists I will remain suspicious. And I will remain unalterably opposed to changes in our methods that I believe are too hasty, too sweeping and too radical for the need.

Mr. Speaker, before coming to the heart of the matter I should like to point out that since the government allotted an amount of some $135,000 or more to the leaders of the parties of the opposition, the members give speeches which, without being more sensible, are better written and can be more easily tolerated. The opposition must recognize that it was a good gesture on the part of the government to give that help.

DEBATES	December 13, 1968
Like several other members, I do not profess to be competent in the matter of parliamentary procedure, but I did make it a point to listen to everything that has been said until now by people who know more about it than I do. I also studied the old Hansards of the house and what other experts have said on parliamentary procedure. I read what the committee on procedure published after its proceedings. I even inquired of the library about what has been done in this regard in other countries, such as Australia and England, for instance. Even so, I do not claim that all this gives me the required competence, but I do say I learned certain things.
This afternoon, I should like to limit my remarks to a rather brief analysis of what has been said until now.
First of all, it seems to me the opposition is overlooking one point when I hear shouts of distress because it would seem that the privileges of parliament are being threatened. It seems to forget that we also belong to parliament, even if our representation spills over onto the other side of the house, and that at the last elections, we were entrusted with the task of governing this country. As far as I know, the results of those elections do not give a minority opposition the absolute right to direct, control, stymie and bog down, to use an expression which is not from Bossuet, the government elected to administer this country.
Mr. Speaker, like many other hon. members I always listen to the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) when he takes the floor. He is a great debater but also a great actor, and I would give him an Oscar for his performances in this house.
The other day while listening to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield)-for whom I have great respect, as I said before, and I think he knows it too-I got the impression that, in view of the success enjoyed by the hon. member for Prince Albert as a public speaker, he would have liked to imitate his tactics or some of his tricks. I would not advise him to try it in view of what has happened so far. The hon. member for Prince Albert has always had that knack for making fun of his opponent, getting him to say what he wants and playing with words with an extraordinary sense of humour, even if he is unkind most of the time. However, experience shows that he has paid for it, because many of his ministers turned against him and his supporters deserted him during election
December 13, 1968	COMMONS
campaigns or political conventions. The leaders of his party have forgotten him and the convention ignored him in a very humiliating way. So the conclusions are so obvious for everyone that, in my opinion, the Leader of the Opposition would venture into a wrong course if he attempted to resort to such debating tricks which are a mere window-dressing, and rather funny. However, these tricks are not consistent, in most cases, with the seriousness of parliament which our friends opposite worship as much as we do.
Mr. Speaker, I think that this whole discussion over the reform of procedure-at least that is what I think and what many other Canadians think-seems to be an organized campaign to throw discredit on the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald) and to present Canadians with a caricature, designed to scare them with the prospect of dictatorship, when the only purpose is to make government efficient, as promised, and that is what Canadians demand of this parliament. I think that many of my friends opposite, perhaps without realizing it, are challenging the Prime Minister, because of his tremendous success and also his main associates and the party now in office.
Mr. Speaker, some people clamour for the respect of parliamentary privileges, but I do not see how these are affected, unless they want to limit the definition of parliament in the sense that the opposition alone would constitute parliament and that the responsibility of controling parliament would rest only with them.
The opposition must say what it has to, and it will have a greater opportunity to do so than before, because for instance the estimates will be scrutinized much more carefully in the parliamentary committees. However, no one should be misled by that outcry which can be heard here under misrepresentations, with a tone which would be moving if it were true, and which seems intended to rescue from ruin or disappearance the privileges of parliament. I will say again that we, of the Liberal Party, also belong to this parliament.
It was said that ordinary members, usually called back-benchers, observe a self-imposed silence. If my friends of the opposition could attend our provincial or federal caucus, they would see that there is truly in our party a freedom of speech promoted by the right honourable Prime Minister, by the whole cabinet and by the President of the Privy Council. Of course, our name is not on the

Motion for Concurrence in Report front page of newspapers the next day, but I think that in the past, in our own way, we contributed to the formulation of legislation and we stopped a man or a party from becoming the government itself. The caucus is precisely democracy in action.
Mr. Speaker, my reaction to the stand taken by the opposition and its comments from the beginning of the debate-and I have listened nearly to all the speeches-is, first of all, that the opposition wants to keep a kind of power to stall legislation so that when election time comes, the government is unable to show a list of achievements which will please the people and which, of course, would induce them to vote for this government. The opposition seems to forget that this government was elected with a very clear mandate: an efficient administration of the business of the state and a reformation of parliamentary procedure in order to get rid of those lengthy speeches which we have deplored for a long time.
The opposition forgets that the Canadian people and in particular the rising young people are fed up with those lengthy and sterile debates which solve nothing. Through his whole speech, my friend, the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier)-I was taking notes-was proposing an acceptable compromise, but in my view his conclusion is not acceptable. I want to point out to him that this is unpractical because in the end, the government would again have the majority and nothing would be changed. Mr. Speaker, many things have been said, and the most striking was said this afternoon by the right hon. member for Prince Albert, who at one time expressed his disapproval in these terms, and I quote:

"A ruthless government can subdue parliament." [Translation]
The right hon. member for Prince Albert, in using the words "ruthless" and "ruthlessness" must have looked at himself in the mirror, because people who were here when he was Prime Minister tell us how determined, how aggressive he was even with the members of his own party. It is hard to conceive that such a thing could happen under the present Prime Minister, Mr. Speaker. As a matter of fact, he often says to us: "Go ahead, say what you have to say." And one day when he was asked

DEBATES	December 13, 1968
what would happen if our free interventions became annoying to a minister, he replied that the ministers must learn to take care of themselves and that if they do not know how to do it, they do not deserve to remain ministers. Up till now, they have taken care of themselves very well, thank God.
And the hon. member for Prince Albert said, while speaking about the President of the Privy Council, and I quote:

"Here is the Simon Legree of parliamentary rights."

This always makes a great deal of impression, Mr. Speaker. Those who hear it for the first time are impressed, it gives them the shudders and brings tears to their eyes. However, when one has heard the member for Prince Albert repeat it twelve times, one feels somewhat less impressed. One tells oneself that it is just some more of his theatricals of which he is a master but which do not settle the situation.
As far as I am concerned, I cannot imagine that the President of the Privy Council could make dictatorial decisions without rousing strong protests among the members of his own party. Let them not take us for school children, for people without a mind of their own, and who do not know what parliament is for. Let them not take us for people who are kneeling down in the hope of getting some day promotions or favours, because we know that there are still a large number of people who think along those lines. It is an exception to be interested in obtaining favours. I will even say that the majority of members on this side have already filled some office in the municipal and provincial fields and on school boards. They are used to parliamentary debates and they respect our par-liamentiary customs. However, they have often heard the rising generation asking for more efficiency and voicing eloquently their disgust for the very costly waste of time in parliament.
Since hon. members must make the parliamentary machinery more efficient, the time has come to complete that reform or it will never be done. I deny that the privileges of members are infringed upon by those measures, except perhaps if one insists that the 264 members of parliament should speak until they are breathless on every possible or conceivable subject. It would then be necessary to sit day and night, 365 days a year. Even
December 13, 1968

then we would not succeed in performing our work.
Mr. Speaker, I heard the member for Prince Albert say:

"The record of this parliament is as good as that of any other parliament."

He then quoted statistics and gave to understand that this parliament has nevertheless achieved something against all odds. Whatever has been accomplished so far does not correspond to the hopes of the Canadian people who are going through changing times characterized by transformation, a true revolution, which requires not only efficient action but also infinitely more numerous and beneficent measures than those adopted so far. That is why our parliamentary procedures must be modernized.
Mr. Speaker, I notice that my allotted time to speak is nearly finished. So that it will not be necessary for you to interrupt me, I conclude my remarks by saying that I approve these measures.

He said: Mr. Speaker, before speaking on this bill I must say that it will indeed be difficult to follow in the footsteps of the illustrious hon. members who preceded me in espousing effervescent rhetoric. It is also ironical that I should be discussing on Friday the 13th a bill which is referred to as Bill C-13, and is listed at page 13 of the order paper. How lucky can I be! Nevertheless I shall endeavour to give in capsule form the purpose and intent of this bill.
Its purpose and intent is basically to eliminate the courts of revision, which generally are established in urban electoral districts, and replace them by the more effective and less costly procedure already provided for
Canada Elections Act
rural voters whereby, on voting day, an elector, whose name does not appear on the official list of electors, may cast his or her ballot, notwithstanding that the name is off the list, upon swearing an oath that he or she is ordinarily a resident of the particular electoral district in question, and meets all other necessary requirements of an elector. This is likewise supported by an oath to the same effect by an elector whose name does appear on the official list of electors, and who is ordinarily a resident of that electoral district, thereby corroborating the previous oath.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
It is proposed that these oaths be administered at any time up to and including the date of an election by the returning officer of the particular district or riding in question, and in addition on election day the returning officer would also be empowered to administer similar oaths, thereby adding, amending or deleting any elector's name on the official list of electors of the electoral district in question.
As I am sure all hon. members are aware, at the present time lists of electors are compiled for each subdivision of an electoral district by enumerators who are appointed by the returning officers of each federal electoral district. These enumerators usually, especially in urban ridings, consist of two persons for each subdivision, one who is usually recommended by the member who is representing that particular riding, and the other who is recommended by the party having the second largest number of votes polled at the previous election for that particular riding. After these lists are compiled copies are made, some of which are placed in conspicuous places in the subdivision for all to view, to see whether their names are on the list. Other copies are given to the returning officer. These lists are required to be completed within a specified time prior to the election date.
In 1934 a system of permanent lists of electors was adopted by parliament for federal elections by the enactment of the Dominion Franchise Act. This system, however, was only enjoyed for the 1935 general election. The Dominion Franchise Act was repealed in 1938, and the system of compiling lists of electors by enumerators, as previously described and referred to, was provided by section 17, as well as schedules A and B of the Dominion Elections Act of 1938. Since that debate the system has been substantially the same, except for the introduction of revising

December 13, 1968
Canada Elections Act
agents to assist the revising officers in revising the electors lists in various districts, particularly in urban areas.
I submit that at the present time the number of persons added to these voters lists by these agents, or these courts of revision, is very small and does not warrant the cost incurred by the public. I should like to submit at this time certain cost figures which I obtained from the Chief Electoral Officer. This is a cost breakdown in respect of the cost of revising these voters lists, and this is up to November 26, 1968. It shows a total cost for the last federal election of $823,658.83. The cost in respect of the metropolitan Toronto area was $63,331.40, and for the metropolitan Montreal area, $77,904.69. I am sure you will agree that this is a little exorbitant.
I should also like to give the house some figures in respect of the Toronto-High Park area. The cost incurred by the revising officers appointed for this area totalled $3,657.41. I am informed that the six courts of revision added to this list some 240 names. In my humble submission this would represent in the vicinity of $15 to $18 for each name added. Surely you will agree that this is costly. There is no reason this task could not be performed by the returning officer and the deputy returning officers. In addition to the cost involved there are other instances of injustice, especially on election day. I personally encountered some of these during the previous election. Residents came to my office and telephoned me, advising that they had attended at their polling booths but were not permitted to vote. It happened that it was pouring rain on the last election day. It is regrettable that people who want to vote in the polling divisions, especially during adverse weather conditions, were not permitted to do so. I asked many of them why they did not get their names on the voters lists in time, and many had very valid reasons. Some said they were out of town and others said that there were a number of persons in the family, some of whom had their names on the list, and they felt their names would also be there; but they failed to check, and when they did find out it was too late.
In other cases these lists were posted on telephone posts or on trees, and may have been torn down by children or destroyed by the elements. In this event some people would not have had the opportunity to view them to make sure their names were included. I submit that the passing of this bill would eliminate these injustices.
tMr. Deakon.]

It used to be the custom that after a dominion election-that is an archaic word which I use-the House of Commons, with the experience that all the members derive from the contest, would sit down, look at the election machinery and make suggested improvements.

I hope it will be done very, very soon so that all questions, that of the voter's age, party affiliations being noted on the ballot, a permanent voters list, and many other aspects of our voting process will be studied, and recommendations made

as a result of which a new act can be brought into being.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)

There are some things about the bill which cause me a little anxiety. However, I do not want my colleagues to forestall the vote because they think I may vote against the measure. The difference between the procedures, as they now exist under the legislation stems from the fact, as I understand it both in practice and from explanation by the experts, that in the rural polls there is little prospect of misrepresentation; that you are not in a situation of anonymity. Where I come from there is a great likelihood that everybody would know everybody else and would have a rough idea how everybody would vote, so telegraphing of votes could not occur in Prince Edward Island. But I have heard of its occurring in other places. We know that devices like this are used in our election process, and we should try to make that process more efficient, fair and honest. Therefore I would be a little leery of this provision. I think the hon. member is to be congratulated for having
Canada Elections Act
introduced the bill. It is a shocking thing when, because of administrative inefficiency, Canadian citizens are denied the right to vote. This question is raised at every election. There are all kinds of people who, because of the failure of an enumerator to do his duty, finds he is denied a vote. This is a shocking thing, because our machinery should be geared to allow every qualified Canadian to exercise his franchise. Yet in election after election the enumerating process fails here and there.
I am sure there is not a constituency in Canada where there has not been embarrassment and upset on the part of qualified voters. Many people-and I say thank God they are like this-take very seriously their right to vote. Many people are deeply disturbed, profoundly upset when they find that this measure of democracy, the freedom of choice, the exercise of selection, is null and void because of the stupidity of some individual or the inadequacy of some regulation or legislation.
I think a better way of dealing with this problem would be to have a permanent voters list where, in the whole period between elections someone is concerned with the problem of keeping the voters list up to date. Once a permanent voters list is established, steps can be taken to overcome the problems with which the hon. gentleman is concerned. A permanent voters list would allow for absentee voting. A permanent voters list would allow with greater ease the transfer of a man's franchise to another election district. We live in a very mobile society and the advance poll although it has been broadened and improved, has not been able to keep up with the fact that many people have moved during the election period. You cannot hold Canadians stationary for the practically two months period of campaigning.
Incidentally, but significantly too, I would think the permanent voters list would allow for a substantially shorter election campaign. Although election campaigning is fun, I think it would not hurt the country a bit if that particular exercise were abbreviated somewhat. I believe, too, that had we a permanent voters list, and if more of the essential process were carried out of having people listed where they belong, and their qualifications certified, more or less in peacetime before the campaign started, there would be better opportunity for some of the officials whom the hon. gentleman mentioned to cope with these last-minute inadequacies, so that people presenting a legitimate case, and who are

December 13, 1968
Canada Elections Act
obviously qualified to vote, can do so. Under our existing machinery they just cannot make it.
In other words, once the court of revision closes, no matter how good is your case, if you are an urbanite you are out of luck at the present time. This is not good. Under our system, when enumerators' lists are completed, hurriedly at certain times, I do not see how the revision offices could be kept open much longer than they are. My more experienced and worldly friends here, the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dins-dale) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), told me that what I was really worrying about was not telescoping votes but telegraphing them. This is a matter which as a political scientist I have studied. I think this would be the one deterrent in the matter. I have not looked into the cost. I had not thought it would be such a money saver, but I would be prepared to study it. It seems to me the revision costs are among the minor ones in the holding of an election.
I commend the hon. gentleman for his initiative. We all join in the desire to broaden the opportunities for people to vote, and to maximize the exercise of citizenship on behalf of Canadians. I think the hon. member has done well in drawing our attention to this matter. I am always happy when in private members hour we are given an opportunity to look at some of the fundamenals of our process. We are doing it in the general debate, but I think we should do it much more often. In this way we can develop a little more awareness of some of the basic aspects of this institution and of the broader institution, namely the democratic process whereby we are brought into being.

He said that himself, and all of us who come from urban centres have had the experience every hour of election day of receiving calls from scores of people who are unable to vote because their names are not on the voters' list. Each new returning officer in every urban constituency vows he will do a better job than the last one, but he does not manage to get a list that has all the names on it. People in urban centres hear about people in rural areas being able to get sworn in on election day. They wonder why they cannot do the same thing.
I agree with the hon. member for Hillsborough that a permanent voters' list, as has been suggested in the report Mr. Castonguay recently made, would be a more logical and better way of solving a problem. However, the member for High Park seems to have come up with a much less costly way of dealing with the matter. It does seem to me it

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak only briefly on this important bill. The hon. member is to be congratulated upon his efforts in this regard. Indeed, it has struck me as being incongruous that in the government's great desire to bring about certain reforms in the operations of this house there has been relatively little activity to date with regard to what I suggest is of even far more concern to Canadians, that is the way in which they participate in the process of governing this country. I think it has been unfortunate that as we have developed many means of mass communication, of making mass decisions, many of which could well involve thousands of responsible Canadians, the only thing still required of most Canadian citizens in terms of the democratic procedures in this country is that once every two, three or four years they go to the polls and make an "X". Then, somehow they have fulfilled their responsibilities as citizens. I think the time is very fast approaching when Canadians are anxious to play a much larger role in their own self-government. We will have to use our imaginations not just the members in this house but the people outside as well, to think of ways in which people can be more actively involved in the process of decision making. The bill with which we are dealing this afternoon is one suggesting an amendment to the election act so that people will not be deprived of their right to vote on election day. I sympathize very much with this sentiment. I believe we are depriving far
Canada Elections Act
too many people of the right to vote on election day. I think it is a remarkable thing that all the Canadians who serve our government in various government departments, with the exception of those who serve in the ranks, have no opportunity to exercise their democratic franchise as citizens of this country on election day if they are outside of the country.
One could even refer to the immediate past prime minister of this country, who for many years was deprived of the exercise of his franchise because he was serving Canada, whether it was in the United States, Great Britain or some other place. I hope that matters such as this will be dealt with very shortly by the Committee on privileges and elections. I hope it will be a very active committee. I hope it will be not only studying legislation referred to it, but I hope the committee will involve many Canadians who have studied this matter and are concerned about it. The widest possible discussion should take place in the committee on privileges and elections. Following that discussion, I hope the government will put on the order paper legislation that will correct many of the inequities we have debated from time to time in this house.
I think, too, of another large group of Canadians that are deprived on a regular basis of their vote on election day. I refer to those who are in hospitals and who, through no fault of their own but because they are incapable of getting to a polling station, are unable to vote. I may say some provinces are more enlightened on this matter than the federal government in that they do permit such people to vote on election day even if they are not able personally to appear at the polls. I think, too, of those who, for one reason or another, while they may not be in hospital, because of some physical infirmity are perhaps unable to get into the polling station. Sometimes it is simply because the polling station may be some steps above ground level and these people have a heart condition or some physical incapacity which prevents them from participating in the election process.
The hon. member for Hillsborough mentioned the fact that we are a very mobile people. I think we forget that roughly a quarter of our population moves every year. There is a space of almost two months between the time of calling the election and the date of the election. During this time people may move, sometimes thousands of miles

December 13, 1968
Canada Elections Act
or more, and they are thereby deprived of their right to vote. If one were able to actually make a count, and it may be worth while for this purpose to determine just how many Canadian citizens are not able to vote in an election, I think we would be both surprised and deeply disturbed. I think it important, therefore, that we consider these matters. Perhaps I may add that we must also be very careful of the rights of Canadians because the secret ballot is something to be guarded carefully.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
I am still troubled by the way in which the service vote is treated as an isolated vote, not usually announced until some days after the general vote has been tabulated and published. It should be possible in this era of high speed communication and transportation, since the service vote is taken some days prior to the general election, to collect this vote, tabulate it and release it as part of the over-all vote for each and every constituency in the country. At the moment I think the situation is unfair to our servicemen. It creates a kind of political aura about the men serving in the ranks, which is not good for them, and certainly not good for the country.
I concur as well with the remarks of the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquar-rie) and his suggestion that there be established a permanent voters list. This is something that has been talked of ad nauseam, yet little has been done to ascertain its cost, as well as the benefits that might accrue, apart from the major benefit that is quite often talked about-shortening the time taken for election campaigns. That would be one virtue.
I also see many other virtues-and this relates to the first point that I made when I rose to speak. If we really believe what we often say in election campaigns, namely that people are more and more anxious to participate, to involve themselves in political questions of the day and to take part in some responsible way in national decision making, then I think by the establishment of a permanent voters list we will recognize the fact that not only are people important at the time of elections-on which we spend a great deal of money, as the hon. member for High Park (Mr. Deakon) pointed out, to tabulate names and publish lists of enumerations-but that people are important to us all of the time. By keeping annual lists of voters we might consider other ways of involving people in the

ongoing decision making process that is self-government.
Generally speaking, Mr. Speaker, I concur with the provisions of this bill, though I think we could improve it a good deal by considering many of the other problems that face us in this regard. I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) who suggested that, if we are to respond to the great desire of the Canadian people today to participate in a realistic way, both in 1968 and beyond, in the process of self-government, the house should approve second reading of this bill, to show our support for these kinds of changes, and then perhaps go on to deal with this bill and other measures in committee in a way that will indicate that we are taking seriously the changes and reforms that are necessary in the elections act.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a certain ritual has developed with respect to private bills, and remarks during this debate reflect that ritual. Some hon. members tried to deal with the principle of the bill while others tried to deal with procedure. I confess to being disappointed with the speech of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) because his entire remarks were devoted to the principle of getting the bill voted on. He did not analyse the contents of the bill, although I know he is well capable of doing so. In some respects I appreciated the remarks of the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) who dealt with the principle of the bill.
The ritual we have developed is this: The mover of the bill says, "We should let this bill come to a vote; it is so unfortunate that so many private members bills are not voted on, and these bills ought to be voted on according to their merits", and so on. Well, Mr. Speaker, at the present time there are more than 100

December 13, 1968
Canada Elections Act
private members bills before the house, and if we were to yield to the ritual each one of our proponents would have us go through, the work of our committees would be substantially changed. Frankly, and I suggest this humbly, I do not think every one of those bills is so carefully drawn that it deserves to be passed in the form in which it is presented to the house.
On the subject of reforming private members hours and abandoning this ritual, perhaps I can tell hon. members what happened in a previous parliament in which I served. A bill similar to the one before us today was part of the package before the house. An hon. member in the house belonging to the party to which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre belongs-he is now a member of the press gallery-had between 15 and 20 private members bills before the house. He gave them exotic names such as "an amendment to the Criminal Code" and so on. From the name he gave a particular bill we could not really know what if was about. One day I listened to him speaking on a bill and, frankly, I could make no sense of it. An hon. member who is now the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources asked the hon. member making the speech if his notes were mixed up, and whether he was not speaking to the wrong bill. It turned out this was correct: The hon. member had gone through half his speech speaking about another bill. He had pulled the wrong file from his cabinet.
The concern I have here is this: I do not believe that the substance of this bill is such that I can support it. I wish to congratulate my colleague from High Park (Mr. Deakon) on his attempt to deal with a Serious problem that we all recognize exists at election times, the problem of the voter who should not have been qualified and has not been qualified, but who shows up at the polls. In a rural poll he can take an oath vouched for by an elector; in an urban poll he cannot. My colleague has therefore argued, and he quoted some convincing material to support his argument, that we should follow the procedure of the rural polls.
I have been a candidate in four elections; in three of them I had a mixed rural and urban constituency with rural and urban polls. May I say that problems with respect to polls differ a great deal in different parts of the country. I had the privilege of serving as a member of the privileges and elections committee when that committee in 1963, 1964 and 1965 held a series of hearings on the Canada

Elections Act. It reported to the house. Unfortunately, because of the log jam of legislation before this house and the difficulty of resolving procedural rules in order to deal with these matters more expeditiously, the proposed legislation was not enacted and the amendments did not come forward in the form we hoped they would.
At this stage, Mr. Speaker, may I put before the house some procedures that deal with the establishment of voters lists. There is good reason for having different procedures in most urban constituencies, as against rural constituencies. In the rural constituency a single enumerator enumerates the voters and prepares lists. In an urban constituency, in the urban polls, there are two enumerators named from the two political interests which received the highest and the second highest number of votes in the previous election. The theory is that these enumerators will watch one another to make sure there is no irregularity and no omission. Each one of them has the opportunity of making observations and comments to his associate doing the same job. The purpose for this is to serve the public interest as carefully as it is possible to do so.
Then comes the revision procedure. Those of us who have worked under it have found it trying and somewhat vexing. But the elimination of courts of revision in my opinion is not the proper answer to what is wrong. I do not care how expensive it is; I am concerned more with questions of principle. If you want to talk about the expense of conducting an election you could talk about the expense of the military vote; you could talk about how expensive it is to try to guarantee that as many Canadians as possible have the right to vote, under circumstances which are compatible with democracy. If we eliminated courts of revision and permitted a very simple procedure on election day, let us think for a moment what we would face.
Let us think of what happened in the last election when there were complaints about revisions of boundaries. In the constituency which I have the honour to represent the boundary runs down the middle of the street, down the middle of Baseline road. Before the previous election it included one strip of houses on the other side of Baseline road. On election day many people found, to their surprise, that they would not be voting in Ottawa West but in Grenville-Carleton, the constituency on the other side of the street.
If you had a simple procedure along the lines of that in rural polls you might get
December 13, 1SS8

something like this: A man might say, "I know John Smith; he lives on Baseline road; I live on Baseline road and I can vouch for him; he has lived there for a long time, is a jolly good chap", and so on. The system just would not work if you did not have in your poll an extremely well qualified deputy returning officer, who would be absolutely informed of the latest boundary revisions of the constituency and thoroughly aware of all the little facts of geography, such as the street here or there that runs down the corner to a cul-de-sac; that it bends just before it gets to the cul-de-sac and that the people in the middle of the cul-de-sac vote in one constituency and those at the end in another constituency. I should have considerable reservations about adopting a system that requires this. I will not use the expression the hon. member for Hillsborough used, but I think hon. members will know what I mean.
The vote of someone not properly qualified to vote is not a proper vote. It is better, Mr. Speaker, that thousands of dollars be spent to make sure that there are no irregularities than that in the interests of economy we should open the door to permit a number of voters who are not properly qualified to swamp election machinery or individual polls by permitting the taking of oaths under the pressure of election day and, if I may say so, thereby possibly subverting the results of such an election.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
The number of circumstances in which hon. members of this house are elected by very small margins is fairly large in the kind of contests we have now. What I am saying is not academic; it is a matter of serious concern to members who are worried about the principles by which we conduct ourselves in democratic elections. In rural constituencies there is a presumption of knowledge. The boundaries of such constituencies are more easily defined-they are not as closely drawn as they are in the great urban centres. Moreover, residents do not change as quickly. It is literally possible to go to a deputy returning officer and say, for instance: The Smiths have not moved out. Why are they not on the list? Everyone knows a mistake has been made, and it is corrected.
There is a certain wisdom which has been accumulated in the Canada Elections Act. It is not a haphazard document. It represents the results of experience during a number of elections conducted in this country at different times. Members of the committees which 29180-250
Canada Elections Act
have examined this problem have come to the conclusion, in their wisdom, that there is necessity for flexible arrangements in the rural areas. This seems to work. There is no great evidence of abuse nor, in my opinion, is there much possibility of abuse as a result of such flexibility. I have not known abuse to take place in the three elections with which I have been concerned although there was a substantial rural population.
I would, however, be gravely concerned about the mechanical difficulty of coping on election day with the number of people who would come to the polls at the boundary of a constituency, especially if those boundaries had been subject to recent change, and claim that they should be put on the list. In many cases they would do so with the best of intentions, in the firm belief that they belonged to a particular constituency, when in fact they did not.
The possibility of irregularities and contested elections arising out of such a situation is very great, in my opinion. As I said before, I am concerned about the way in which previous speakers have dealt with the subject matter of the bill. Although this subject is one which causes me concern personally, I don't believe the direction they have indicated is one I should like to see this legislation take. I may be wrong, but if I recall correctly the evidence given before the committee by Mr. Castonguay, who is experienced in these matters and who has the complete confidence of all parties in this house, it was not such as to prompt those of us who were members of the committee to move to include this type of amendment in the act. The committee did not deal lightly with the measure, and for this reason I personally feel that in the circumstances I cannot support the principle of the bill.
